original_value: Network intrusion detection is a relatively mature research topic, but one that remains challenging particular as technologies and threat landscape evolve. Here, a semi-supervised tri-Adaboost (STA) algorithm is proposed. In the algorithm, three different Adaboost algorithms are used as the weak classifiers (both for continuous and categorical data), constituting the decision stumps in the tri-training method. In addition, the chi-square method is used to reduce the dimension of feature and improve computational efficiency. We then conduct extensive numerical studies using different training and testing samples in the KDDcup99 dataset and discover the flows demonstrated that (1) high accuracy can be obtained using a training dataset which consists of a small number of labeled and a large number of unlabeled samples. (2) The algorithm proposed is reproducible and consistent over different runs. (3) The proposed algorithm outperforms other existing learning algorithms, even with only a small amount of labeled data in the training phase. (4) The proposed algorithm has a short execution time and a low false positive rate, while providing a desirable detection rate.

result.paraphrase: Network intrusion detection is a relatively mature research area, yet it remains difficult as technologies and the threat landscape continue to evolve. This work proposes a semi-supervised tri-Adaboost (STA) algorithm. It uses three different AdaBoost algorithms as weak classifiers for both continuous and categorical data, forming the decision stumps in the tri-training approach. The chi-square method is also applied to reduce feature dimensionality and improve computational efficiency. Extensive numerical experiments on the KDDcup99 dataset with various training and testing samples show that: (1) high accuracy can be achieved with a training set containing few labeled samples and many unlabeled ones; (2) the proposed algorithm is reproducible and consistent across runs; (3) it outperforms existing learning algorithms even when only a small amount of labeled data is available during training; and (4) it has short execution time and a low false positive rate while maintaining a desirable detection rate.
